attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post, stated as his assessment.

semantics.note: Matches the statement and keeps the deepfake-porn exception. 'Passed almost no legislation' is a fair paraphrase of 'done almost nothing legislatively'.

contract.note: Reading 'the US' as federal law is an ordinary reading, but Marcus did not limit it that way, and state laws such as Colorado's would change the picture. 'Almost nothing' has no threshold, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: CRS report dated June 4, 2025, just after the post. It says no broad federal AI law exists and that Congress passed mainly targeted provisions. That leans toward the claim on a federal reading, but it is a snapshot from after the target date.
AI Training Act (2022) mandates risk training for the federal acquisition workforce. It is a real exception outside deepfake porn but narrow, so it does not by itself disprove 'almost nothing'.
Colorado SB24-205 (2024) is an enforceable state law on algorithmic discrimination. It matters if 'the US' includes the states; on the federal reading it is only context.

reviews.rationale: On the federal reading the evidence leans toward support: one narrow federal law, plus a CRS finding of targeted provisions only. But there is no authoritative inventory dated before the post, the additional procurement safeguards were not provided as evidence items, and the state-law reading (Colorado) cuts against the claim. The packet does not settle whether the record amounts to 'almost nothing'.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Mostly faithful. It drops 'in my view' from the 'greatly flawed' part, which is opinion, and narrows 'companies like OpenAI and Anthropic' to those two. The causal part (distraction, more power) is kept.

contract.note: Asking for evidence of the stated distraction and power effects is a fair test. 'Greatly flawed' is evaluative and cannot really be scored.

evidence.note: The AI 2027 authors' own page, inviting debate. It states their intent, not what audiences actually did, so it neither supports nor contradicts the causal claim.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no audience study, investor record, or policy record showing that AI 2027 distracted attention from the companies' flaws or increased their influence. The authors' invitation to criticism says nothing about the actual effects. The claim cannot be settled on this packet.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'so far' and both parts: labor market and measurable productivity.

contract.note: Reading the claim as about broad, aggregate effects fits the surrounding argument about economic transformation. 'Modest' has no number, so where the line falls affects the result.

evidence.note: Danish administrative data through December 2024, inside the target period. It finds near-zero effects on earnings, hours, and employment. That supports the labor-market part, but only for Denmark.
St. Louis Fed survey: self-reported time savings of about 1.4% of all hours. A model-based guess at aggregate productivity is not a measured statistic, so this is context only.
Single-firm study of a 2020–21 rollout, showing a gain of about 15% in chats handled per hour. It cuts against a literal reading of 'any' statistic, but one firm cannot show an aggregate effect.

reviews.rationale: The labor-market part is supported by the Danish administrative study, though only for one country. The contract requires evidence on both parts, and the packet has no realized aggregate productivity measurement: e2 is self-reported and model-based, and e3 covers one firm. The claim as a whole stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithfully turns the 'wind in their sails' metaphor into a present-tense causal claim about money and political power.

contract.note: Requiring that any effect be attributable to AI 2027, rather than pointing to general funding growth, is fair. The contradiction condition rightly says that failing to find attribution does not count as contradiction.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own disclosure of its March 3, 2025 funding round. That round came before AI 2027 was published on April 3, 2025, so AI 2027 cannot have caused it, and the release makes no such attribution.

reviews.rationale: No investor or policy record in the packet links any financing or political influence to AI 2027. The only item is a funding round that came before the scenario was published. There is no evidence either way on the causal claim.
